topics.title: Muscle, Connective Tissue and Tenderness
topics.short: Muscles that worked hard (shoulder, leg) have more connective tissue and want slow moist heat; tender ones (loin, rib) want quick dry heat. Slice across the grain.
topics.trouble: Cooks grill a tough cut fast or braise a tender loin for hours and dry it out.

topics.title: Beef, Pork and Lamb Primal Cuts
topics.short: Butchers split each carcass into primals (beef: chuck, rib, short loin, sirloin, round, brisket, plate, flank), then subprimals and portions.
topics.trouble: Learners think a cut's name tells its cooking method without knowing where it comes from on the animal.

topics.title: Brines, Marinades and Rubs
topics.short: A brine is salt dissolved in water by weight; it seasons inside and helps meat hold moisture. Marinades flavor the surface. Keep both refrigerated and discard used raw marinade unless boiled.
topics.trouble: Cooks brine in a weak or extra-strong solution by guessing volume, or baste with marinade that held raw chicken.

topics.title: Breaking Down a Chicken
topics.short: Legs off at the joint, thighs from drumsticks, breasts off the bone, wings at the joint: eight pieces, plus a frame for stock. Work clean and sanitize after.
topics.trouble: Beginners saw through bone instead of finding the joint with the knife tip.

topics.title: Fish: Freshness and Filleting a Round Fish
topics.short: Fresh fish smells like the sea, has firm flesh and bright, clear eyes. A round fish gives two fillets: cut behind the head, then along the backbone.
topics.trouble: Cooks press too hard and leave half the flesh on the frame, or forget to pull pin bones.

topics.title: Shellfish Basics
topics.short: Live clams, mussels and oysters have closed shells or close when tapped; discard any that stay open or are cracked; keep shellstock tags 90 days; cook shrimp and lobster until opaque.
topics.trouble: Cooks store live shellfish in sealed plastic or fresh water, which kills them.

topics.title: Doneness, Resting and Carryover Cooking
topics.short: Meat keeps rising in temperature after it leaves the heat, a few degrees for steaks and more for big roasts; pull early, rest, then slice.
topics.trouble: Cooks pull a roast at the final temperature they want and end up several degrees past it.

topics.title: Eggs: Omelets and Poaching
topics.short: The French omelet is rolled, pale and creamy; the American omelet is folded and lightly browned. Poach in barely simmering water; egg dishes are safe at 160°F.
topics.trouble: Cooks use too much heat, so the omelet browns and toughens before it sets.
